setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and want to move up to a higher-level job within a year.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you have decided you want a promotion in the next year.
pressure: {coworker3} says promotions mostly come down to luck.
A friend says you should just apply everywhere and see what happens.
detail: You have worked here for about a year.
Your current job is going well.

tiers.1: Your health has to be sustainable before you add new goals.
tiers.2: Knowing what your supervisor thinks you need shapes every other step.
tiers.3: A clear, measurable goal turns a wish into a plan.
tiers.4: A required qualification has to be planned for early.
tiers.5: Using available benefits makes the plan easier once it is set.

fact: You have worked extra shifts for six weeks straight and feel exhausted most days.
issues.action: Talk with {lead|the} about a more sustainable schedule before taking on new goals.
issues.reason: Exhaustion makes every other goal harder and can harm your health. A sustainable schedule comes first.
issues.lesson: Take care of your wellness so your career goals are sustainable.

shortcut.text: Add evening classes on top of the extra shifts to move up faster.
shortcut.why: Piling more onto an exhausting schedule risks your health and your performance.
shortcut.mis: Working harder always speeds up a career.

fact: You do not know what {lead|the} thinks you would need to improve to be promoted.
clear: {Lead|the} told you last week that leading a small project is your next step.
issues.done: {lead|the} already told you what to work on
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} for specific feedback on what you would need to develop.
issues.reason: Your supervisor knows what the next job requires. Their feedback points your effort where it counts.
issues.lesson: Ask for specific feedback about what advancement requires.

shortcut.text: Guess what matters and start working on that.
shortcut.why: Guessing may spend months on the wrong skills.
shortcut.mis: You already know what your supervisor values.

fact: Your written goal says only "get better at my job."
clear: You already wrote a goal with a specific measure and a date.
issues.done: your goal is already specific, measurable and dated
issues.action: Rewrite the goal so it is specific, measurable, realistic and has a deadline.
issues.brief: rewrite the goal as a SMART goal
issues.reason: A vague goal gives you nothing to plan or measure. A SMART goal shows what to do and when you have succeeded.
issues.lesson: Write goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

shortcut.text: Keep the goal broad so you cannot fail it.
shortcut.why: A goal you cannot fail is also a goal you cannot measure or plan for.
shortcut.mis: Broad goals are safer than specific ones.

fact: The posting for the higher-level job lists a certification you do not have yet.
issues.action: Find out what the certification takes and add it to your plan with dates.
issues.brief: plan for the certification with dates
issues.reason: Required qualifications can take months. Planning early means you can be ready when a position opens.
issues.lesson: Learn what qualifications advancement requires and plan to earn them.

shortcut.text: Apply anyway and hope the certification is not checked.
shortcut.brief: apply and hope it is not checked
shortcut.why: Listed requirements are usually checked. Applying without a plan wastes the opportunity.
shortcut.mis: Requirements in job postings are only suggestions.

clear: You already enrolled in the certification course that starts next month.
issues.done: you are already enrolled in the course

fact: The employee handbook says the company pays for job-related courses, but you have not looked into it.
clear: You already confirmed the company will pay for your course.
issues.done: the course benefit was already confirmed
issues.action: Read that handbook section and ask {lead|the} how to apply for the benefit.
issues.reason: A benefit you do not use is money left on the table. It may cover a course you need.
issues.lesson: Know the benefits and resources your employer offers, and use them.

shortcut.text: Pay for courses yourself, since asking about benefits seems pushy.
shortcut.why: Benefits are part of your pay. Asking about them is normal and professional.
shortcut.mis: Using benefits makes you look demanding.

proceed.text: Follow your written plan and check your progress each month.
proceed.why: Your plan is clear, supported and sustainable, so steady progress and regular check-ins are next.
proceed.lesson: With a clear plan in place, act on it and track your progress.

generic.text: Quit and look for a higher-level job somewhere else right away.
generic.why: Leaving without a plan or the needed qualifications does not solve the gap.

generic.text: Wait for {lead|the} to offer you a promotion.
generic.why: Advancement usually takes planning and asking. Waiting leaves your career to chance.
generic.mis: Good work is always noticed and rewarded without asking.

overcaution.text: Put the plan on hold until you feel completely ready.
overcaution.why: The plan is ready now. Waiting for a perfect moment delays progress.
overcaution.mis: You should feel completely ready before starting.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, planning how to earn a promotion within a year.

feedback: You have not asked {lead|the} what you would need to improve.
cert: The higher-level job lists a certification you have not earned.
benefit: The handbook mentions a course benefit you have not checked.

steps.text: Work on the plan each week

rel: Feedback tells you what the goal should target.
You act on the plan once the goal is set.
The certification fits into the goal's plan.
Check whether the course is paid for before enrolling.
The course is part of the weekly work.
You review progress after working on the plan.
process.lesson: Get feedback, set a SMART goal, line up resources, act, and review.

title: Your one-year career plan
intro: You are reviewing your draft career plan before sharing it with {lead|the}.
doc.lesson: A strong career plan has a measurable goal, realistic steps and dates, and uses available support.

lines.text: Goal: be ready to apply for the higher-level job by next September.
Measure: complete the required certification and lead one project.
lines.fine: Measurable targets tied to the job requirements.

bad.text: Measure: feel more confident at work.
bad.why: A feeling cannot be measured. The plan needs concrete targets.

lines.text: Step 1: enroll in the certification course in January.

bad.text: Step 1: enroll in a course someday.
bad.why: "Someday" is not a step anyone can plan around; the plan needs a date.

lines.text: Cost: covered by the company course benefit, confirmed with {lead|the}.
Time: about three hours a week, which fits my current schedule.

bad.text: Time: finish the whole certification this weekend.
bad.why: A certification that takes months cannot be finished in a weekend. The plan needs realistic steps.

lines.text: Check-in: review progress with {lead|the} every two months.
lines.fine: Regular review keeps the plan on track.

bad.text: Check-in: none needed until I apply.
bad.why: Without check-ins, problems are not caught until it is too late.

review.notes: Course benefit stated as a handbook policy. No claims about laws or specific benefit rules.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and just got your second paycheck.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are sorting out your pay and benefits after your first month.
pressure: A friend says budgeting is only for people with big paychecks.
detail: You get paid every two weeks.
You started this job a month ago.

tiers.1: A benefit deadline that is about to pass comes first.
tiers.2: Understand your pay before you plan with it.
tiers.3: A budget turns a paycheck into a plan.
tiers.4: A costly credit decision deserves careful thought before smaller daily habits.
tiers.5: Daily wellness habits matter once the urgent money questions are handled.

fact: Enrollment for the workplace health plan closes Friday, and you have not chosen yet.
issues.action: Review the plan options and enroll before Friday's deadline.
issues.reason: Missing the enrollment deadline can mean waiting months for coverage.
issues.lesson: Know your benefit deadlines and act before they pass.

shortcut.text: Wait until you get sick to decide about the plan.
shortcut.why: Coverage usually has to be chosen before you need it.
shortcut.mis: Benefits can be picked up anytime.

clear: You already enrolled in the health plan last week.

fact: Your paycheck is lower than you expected, and you have not read the deductions.
issues.action: Read the deductions on your pay stub and ask payroll about anything unclear.
issues.brief: read the deductions and ask payroll
issues.reason: Deductions such as taxes and benefits explain the difference. Understanding them prevents surprises.
issues.lesson: Read your pay stub and understand each deduction.

shortcut.text: Assume payroll made a mistake and complain to {lead|the}.
shortcut.why: Most differences come from normal deductions; read the stub first.
shortcut.mis: A smaller check always means an error.

clear: Payroll already explained each deduction on your stub.

fact: You have no plan for how your pay covers rent, food and savings.
issues.action: Write a simple monthly budget for needs, savings and wants.
issues.reason: A budget shows whether your pay covers your needs and helps you save on purpose.
issues.lesson: Plan how your pay will be spent and saved.

shortcut.text: Spend as you go and see what is left at the end of the month.
shortcut.why: Without a plan, savings and bills can come up short.
shortcut.mis: Budgets are only needed when money runs out.

clear: You already wrote a simple monthly budget.

fact: A store offers a credit card with high interest in exchange for 10 percent off today.
issues.action: Skip the card unless you are sure you can pay the full balance each month.
issues.brief: skip the card unless you pay in full
issues.reason: High interest can quickly cost more than the one-time discount saves.
issues.lesson: Compare the long-term cost of credit with the short-term savings.

shortcut.text: Sign up, since 10 percent off is free money.
shortcut.why: The discount is one-time; interest on any unpaid balance keeps adding up.
shortcut.mis: Store discounts make credit cards free.

fact: You have been skipping breaks to finish work faster.
issues.action: Take your scheduled breaks so you stay healthy and focused.
issues.reason: Breaks help you stay healthy and focused, which supports good work over time.
issues.lesson: Build habits that keep you healthy at work.

shortcut.text: Keep skipping breaks, since it shows dedication.
shortcut.why: Skipping breaks wears you down and can lower your work quality.

proceed.text: Stick with the budget and benefit choices you have made.
proceed.why: Your benefits, pay and budget are in order, so following your plan is next.
proceed.lesson: Once your plan is set, follow it and review it now and then.

generic.text: Borrow money from coworkers until the next paycheck.
generic.why: Borrowing from coworkers strains relationships and does not fix the plan.
generic.mis: Coworkers are a good source of loans.

generic.text: Ignore the paperwork until someone reminds you.
generic.why: Deadlines and deductions do not wait for reminders.

overcaution.text: Ask payroll to explain your stub again every pay period.
overcaution.why: The deductions were already explained; repeating the question wastes time.
overcaution.mis: You can never ask about pay too often.

review.notes: Enrollment deadline stated in the scenario. General personal-finance guidance, no tax or legal claims.
